question: When oil becomes an imperial commodity, who supplies it, who is barred from it — and where do pressing and churning begin elsewhere?
thesis: Between 300 BC and 600 AD, fat moves by every channel there is. Within Rome’s own empire, provinces feed the capital; between empires, the Periplus carries Indian ghee and sesame oil to Rome and Africa; across continents, sesame reaches China by the Silk Road; and when the western empire falls, butter enters Europe by conquest, not trade. India and China also each begin building a market and a kitchen around oil in these same centuries — oil earning a place beside ghee in India, and the first pressing appearing in China — but in neither place does it yet replace the animal fat it sits beside.

big_ideas.title: Rome feeds its capital from its own provinces
big_ideas.text: Monte Testaccio’s fifty million jars, the Tripolitanian boom, an official for the oil annona, Caesar’s fine on Leptis, and a rule of thumb that puts the Mediterranean’s need at hundreds of millions of litres a year.

big_ideas.title: The Hellenistic world taxes, prices and reveres its own oil
big_ideas.text: Ptolemy taxes five oils, Delos’s temple rents rise and fall with the oil price, the Fayum names seven different oils, and a legend turns one day’s lamp oil into eight — a ritual that travels with a people rather than a cargo.

big_ideas.title: India’s ghee and oil travel west
big_ideas.text: The Periplus carries ghee and sesame oil from Indian ports to Rome and the African coast, while at home the Arthaśāstra prices oil in the meat shop and Caraka and Suśruta give oil a place in medicine — a market and a medicine growing up beside ghee, not replacing it.

big_ideas.title: Sesame travels the Silk Road into China
big_ideas.text: Sesame travels the Silk Road under the Han; pressing itself is first recorded only afterward, on an argument from silence; and by 544 AD a commercial oil trade exists, yet the same manual says lard and tallow are still preferred for roasting and frying.

big_ideas.title: The barbarian’s fat takes Rome’s place
big_ideas.text: Galen calls butter the fat of cold regions without olive oil; a Gallo-Roman bishop complains of a Burgundian with rancid butter in his hair; a Byzantine physician at a Gothic court prescribes it as medicine; and Mueller reads the Germanic conquest as animal fat’s revenge on imperial oil.

threads.title: Rome feeds its capital from its own provinces
threads.claim: Oil moves from provincial press to imperial jar to a state office built to manage the flow.

beats.text: Mago of Carthage writes the farming manual in Punic that Rome later has translated.
Cato describes the beam press, and Pliny lists the screw press and the roller mill.
Caesar fines Leptis three million pounds of oil after the civil war.
Monte Testaccio rises from over 50 million amphorae, mostly from southern Spain.
About 20 litres a head would make the Mediterranean’s need 500 to 1,000 million litres a year.
The territory of Lepcis holds perhaps 1,500 olive presses, and its elite grows rich on oil.
Tripolitanian oil reaches Rome and Ostia in its own amphorae, stamped by elite estates.
Lepcis’s gift of oil to Rome leads to a procurator for the Tripolitanian oil annona.

threads.title: The Hellenistic world taxes, prices and reveres its own oil
threads.claim: East of Rome, oil is taxed, priced into rent, and kept sacred, by states that are themselves successors of Alexander’s conquest.

beats.text: On Delos, farms with no olives pay rents that rise and fall with the price of oil.
Ptolemy II’s Revenue Laws tax five oils, among them castor.
The Fayum papyri name castor, linseed, radish, safflower, sesame and olive oil.
In tradition, one day’s lamp oil lights the Temple Menorah for eight days.

threads.title: India’s ghee and oil travel west
threads.claim: Indian oil reaches Rome and Africa as cargo, while at home it earns a documented place beside ghee.

beats.text: The Pali Vinaya lets sick monks take ghee, butter, oil, honey and syrup after midday.
The Periplus lists ghee and sesame oil among goods carried from Indian ports to the African coast.
Caraka advises ghee in autumn and sesame oil for frying; Suśruta counts sixty oilseeds.
The Arthaśāstra gives the oil, curds and spices for dressing 20 palas of meat in a shop.

threads.title: Sesame travels the Silk Road into China
threads.claim: A crop moves west to east along the Silk Road, and pressing itself follows, centuries later, without displacing animal fat.

beats.text: Tradition says Zhang Qian brings sesame from the west along the Silk Road.
Needham concludes that pressing seeds for oil was not accomplished until the late Han.
A warehouse holds ten thousand piculs of hemp oil, a record of oil as a trade commodity.
The Chhi min yao shu has colza seed sold to the oil mills, worth as much as hulled grain.
The same manual teaches how to churn su, China’s butter-like fat, from soured milk.

threads.title: The barbarian’s fat takes Rome’s place
threads.claim: The line the Mediterranean drew between civilised oil and barbarian butter is crossed when the barbarians conquer.

beats.text: Galen says people in cold regions without olive oil wash with butter, and that doctors use it in poultices.
The Germanic peoples bring a cuisine of meat, beer and animal fat in place of bread, wine and oil.
Sidonius Apollinaris complains of a Burgundian with his head ‘perfumed with rancid butter’.
The physician Anthimus prescribes fresh unsalted butter with honey for consumption.

turning_points.text: Ptolemy II taxes five oils in Egypt.
Mago’s Punic farming manual is written.
Cato describes the beam press for olives.
Sesame is said to reach China by the Silk Road.
Caesar fines Leptis three million pounds of oil.
The Periplus carries Indian ghee and sesame oil to Rome and Africa.
Monte Testaccio grows to over 50 million jars.
China’s first pressing is dated, on an argument from silence.
Indian medicine gives oil a season of its own, beside ghee.
Rome appoints an official for Tripolitania’s oil annona.
The Germanic peoples bring animal fat into the western empire.
China’s own manual still prefers lard and tallow even as its oil trade matures.

text: Rome as consumer and administrator: the jars of Monte Testaccio, the per-head figure, the beam and screw presses, soap as a cosmetic, Gaul’s butter, Galen and Anthimus on butter, Delos’s rents and the Germanic shift ([[ec1]], [[ec3]], [[te1]], [[te3]], [[e1]], [[th1]], [[th2]], [[ec6]], [[w1]]).

Three entries: Ptolemy II’s tax on five oils in Egypt, the oils named in the Greek papyri of the Fayum, and the Hanukkah lamp-oil legend ([[o1]], [[ec8]], [[b2]]). Egypt is filed here by the atlas taxonomy, though the Tripolitanian and Punic oils are North African.

India and China each begin their own fat story: the Buddha’s five medicines, Caraka on ghee, the Arthaśāstra shop, the Periplus’s exports; China learns to press seeds and churn su, and sesame arrives by the Silk Road ([[b1]], [[th3]], [[ec5]], [[x3]], [[te2]], [[te4]], [[th4]], [[ec4]], [[x2]]).

Five entries: Carthage and Tripolitania seen from Rome — Mago’s manual, Caesar’s fine on Leptis, the oil gift to Rome, the olive boom and Tripolitanian oil in Rome ([[th5]], [[o2]], [[o3]], [[ec2]], [[x1]]). The exchange thread’s own Periplus entry (filed under the Far East, since it starts from India) also names the African ports as the Indian ghee and sesame oil’s destination. Sub-Saharan Africa’s own fat economy, as opposed to what the Mediterranean and Indian Ocean worlds shipped to or past it, still has no entry.

One entry, and an isolated one: Hopewell peoples in the Mississippi and Illinois valleys grow sumpweed and sunflower as oilseed crops, reaching their peak under the Kansas City Hopewell culture. Nothing here connects it to the folio’s channels of movement — it is a parallel, independent development, not a trade good or a conquest.
One entry: the domesticated coconut carried by Polynesians, whose ancestral culture emerged in Tonga and Samoa in the second half of the first millennium BC ([[ec7]]).

sources.intro: A scholarly archaeology of Roman oil in Mattingly, a scholarly translation of Chinese farm and oil texts in Needham, popular histories for butter, and Achaya for India.
main: Mattingly, *Tripolitania* and ‘The Olive Boom’, for the Libyan estates, amphorae and annona ([[ec1]], [[ec2]], [[o2]], [[o3]], [[x1]], [[ec3]]).
Needham, SCC 6.5, for the Chinese presses, oils and su ([[te1]], [[te2]], [[ec4]], [[th4]], [[te4]]).
Achaya for India ([[th3]], [[ec5]], [[x3]]); Khosrova and Mueller for Rome's butter and the Germanic shift ([[th1]], [[th2]], [[e1]], [[w1]]); Dalby for Egypt ([[o1]]).
Foxhall for Delos ([[ec6]]); Mueller for Hanukkah ([[b2]]); encyclopedia and lecture notes found by search for Mago ([[th5]]); Kiple for the coconut ([[ec7]]).
Lucas, read from a scanned copy, for Egypt’s oils in the Greek papyri ([[ec8]]).
Wikipedia and the Ohio History Connection for Hopewell’s sumpweed economy ([[ec9]]).
contested: Whether Caesar's fine was annual and which Leptis it fell on ([[o2]]); the Arthaśāstra's date ([[ec5]]).
The first pressing of oil in China is an argument from absence ([[te2]]).
The Germanic ‘revenge of animal fat’ is Mueller's interpretation ([[w1]]).
Dating of the Monte Testaccio dump is the folio's, not a cited figure ([[ec1]]).
Mago’s date is unsettled ([[th5]]); Mueller dates the Hanukkah miracle to 168 BC, where 164 BC is the usual year ([[b2]]); the coconut entry’s date is a placeholder ([[ec7]]).
The sumpweed entry rests on web summaries, not the original archaeobotanical papers; the likely source (Bruce Smith, 1987) was found only as an unreadable scanned image ([[ec9]]).
gaps: Roman literary sources (Cato, Columella, Pliny) were not read directly; nor the Egyptian papyri.
Soap in antiquity rests on two passing mentions ([[te3]]).
Sub-Saharan Africa has no entry in this folio; the shea sequence at Kirikongo starts about 100 AD and is filed in the next folio ([[ec7]] in fats-600-1000).

Buddhism’s and Jainism’s ahimsa really did reshape Indian diet over the centuries, and Buddhist vegetarianism really did reshape Chinese cooking — but neither belongs in this folio. India’s shift is a centuries-long drift with no single mechanism in the sources held (Achaya’s own chapter on meat and vegetarianism gives no economic cause, and warns that the pilgrims’ ‘almost universal vegetarianism’ is an exaggeration: about 25–30 per cent of Indians are vegetarian even today). China’s formal monastic vegetarianism is usually dated to Emperor Wu of Liang’s edicts of the 510s–520s, and the wheat-gluten and bean-curd meat-substitute cuisine Anderson describes is explicitly Tang dynasty, not yet known even in the 840s. Both stories belong in the next folio or two, sourced to Achaya and Anderson.

how_to_read: Read the thesis and the big ideas first, then the threads: each runs in date order and points to the entries that carry it. Entries that no thread needs are still reached through the regional picture and the lists.
The Roman entries sit in *Economy*, *Order* and *Technology*; the Indian and Chinese ones in *Thought*. Read the Nexus for the Tripolitanian chain from estates to jars to Rome.
Note the numbers: they are Mattingly's and Foxhall's estimates, not Roman records, and their tier labels say so.

The *picture by region* counts the 28 entries: Europe 9, Near East 3, Far East 9, Africa 5, Americas 1, Oceania 1; none in Worldwide. Africa here is the Roman oil province seen from Rome, not the home of African fats.
before: The last folio ended with fat as an institution in one place at a time: Greek law, Vedic ritual, a Near Eastern workshop. This folio is where fat starts crossing the boundaries that institution drew.
after: The next folio carries Rome’s oil habits into the Islamic Mediterranean and the Geniza trade network, while China’s and India’s oil economies mature and Europe settles into the butter economy that conquest brought it.
